### Entry Timing Against a Common Path {#sec-vintage-exposure-iv}

Many economic states are not chosen in one go. They are the product of a decision made once, at
some entry date, and a common path that everyone experiences afterward. A homeowner chooses a
purchase date and a down payment; the local price index does the rest, and together they fix
home equity years later. A borrower locks a mortgage rate at origination; the market rate path
then decides how far below market that rate sits. A worker graduates in some year; the business
cycle decides what the labor market looks like at entry. In each case the state we care about is
endogenous if we look at it directly, because the people with high equity, cheap mortgages, or
lucky graduation years differ from everyone else. But the state is built from two pieces, and
the research design can lean on whichever piece is closer to as-good-as-random.

This section develops that idea through @liao2026whats, which asks whether home equity changes
how much flood risk a homeowner is willing to carry uninsured. The paper is worth studying
closely for two reasons. It uses two distinct designs, one aggregate and one micro, that borrow
variation from the same housing cycle in different ways. And its micro design does something
more ambitious than the usual instrument: it separates two causal channels that move together
almost one for one, by exploiting the fact that the same shock to equity maps into very
different changes in the quantity that matters, depending on when a household bought.

#### Two Channels That Move Together

Higher home equity could raise flood insurance demand for two reasons. The first is a wealth
effect: richer households buy more insurance, a pattern documented for other lines of coverage
even though textbook expected-utility models predict the opposite sign. The second is risk
shifting. A homeowner with a mortgage holds something like a call option on the house. If a flood
destroys the structure and the damage exceeds the owner's equity, the owner can walk away and
hand the loss to the lender. Default then works as implicit insurance with a deductible equal to
the owner's equity plus whatever default costs. The idea has a close relative in health
insurance, where @mahoney2015bankruptcy shows that the option to file for bankruptcy crowds out
demand for formal coverage, and in housing, where negative equity reduces homeowners' investment
in their properties [@melzer2017mortgage] and changes their labor supply
[@bernstein2021negative].

The paper makes the risk-shifting channel measurable. Let $L$ be the flood loss as a share of the
structure value $S$, with distribution $f(\ell)$ conditional on a flood, and let $E$ be home
equity. A homeowner who defaults whenever losses exceed equity bears

$$
\text{EaR}(E, S) = \sum_{\ell} f(\ell)\, \min\big(\max(E, 0),\ \ell S\big),
$$

which the authors call equity-at-risk. EaR is the expected flood loss that actually lands on
the homeowner. It is flat in $E$ when equity exceeds the structure value (the owner never wants
to default, so bears every loss) and flat again when equity is negative (the owner bears nothing).
In between it rises, but less than one for one. The whole design turns on that nonlinearity.

A numerical illustration shows why. Take two identical houses, each with a structure worth
\$150,000, and suppose local prices fall enough between 2007 and 2012 to erase \$60,000 of
equity for every owner in the market. One owner bought early in the boom and holds \$180,000 of
equity at the peak; after the bust she still has \$120,000 and still bears nearly all of any
flood loss. The other bought at the peak with a small down payment and holds \$70,000; after the
bust he has \$10,000, and a total loss would now cost him only that. Both lost the same wealth.
Only the second lost most of his stake in the flood outcome. If insurance demand responds to EaR
and not merely to wealth, the second owner should drop coverage and the first should not.

```{r vint-kink-figure, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "Equity-at-risk as a function of home equity for a \\$150,000 structure. Both owners lose \\$60,000 of equity in the bust. The early buyer stays on the flat upper segment and keeps almost all of her flood exposure; the peak buyer slides down the steep segment and sheds most of his."}
library(ggplot2)

# Conditional flood-loss distribution on a 1 percent grid of structure value.
# Most claims are small relative to the structure; a thin tail reaches total loss.
l_grid <- seq(0.01, 1, by = 0.01)
f_l <- dbeta(l_grid, 0.5, 1.6)
f_l <- f_l / sum(f_l)
ear <- function(equity, structure) {
  vapply(seq_along(equity), function(i)
    sum(f_l * pmin(pmax(equity[i], 0), l_grid * structure[i])), numeric(1))
}

S <- 150
curve_df <- data.frame(equity = seq(-40, 220, by = 1))
curve_df$ear <- ear(curve_df$equity, rep(S, nrow(curve_df)))

owners <- data.frame(
  who    = rep(c("Early buyer", "Peak buyer"), each = 2),
  when   = rep(c("2007", "2012"), 2),
  equity = c(180, 120, 70, 10)
)
owners$ear <- ear(owners$equity, rep(S, 4))

ggplot(curve_df, aes(equity, ear)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_path(data = owners, aes(group = who, colour = who),
            arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm")), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = owners, aes(colour = who), size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Early buyer" = "#2C7FB8", "Peak buyer" = "#D95F0E")) +
  labs(x = "Home equity ($1,000)", y = "Equity-at-risk ($1,000)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r vint-kink-numbers}
data.frame(owner = c("Early buyer", "Peak buyer"),
           change_in_equity = c(-60, -60),
           change_in_EaR = round(c(owners$ear[2] - owners$ear[1],
                                   owners$ear[4] - owners$ear[3]), 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "The same wealth loss, very different losses of skin in the game (thousands of dollars).")
```

The identification problem now has a clean shape. Equity and EaR are both endogenous, since
both depend on income, down payment, and where and when a household chose to buy. And even with
a perfect instrument for equity, one instrument cannot separate two channels. What the authors
need is variation in EaR holding the change in equity fixed, which is exactly what the figure
displays.

#### Design One: Structural Breaks in Local Price Paths

The aggregate half of the paper estimates the total effect of home prices on flood insurance
take-up across metropolitan areas, without yet separating channels. The endogeneity problem is
familiar. Metropolitan areas where prices rose fastest may also have had rising incomes,
population inflows, or new construction in floodplains, all of which move insurance demand
directly.

The instrument comes from the anatomy of the 2000s boom. @ferreira2023anatomy document that
many metropolitan price series show a sharp, discrete acceleration at a specific quarter in the
early 2000s, while others rise smoothly throughout. Fundamentals such as wages, employment, and
construction costs do not break at those dates. @charles2018housing turn this into an instrument:
fit a single trend break to each area's price series over 2001 to 2005 and take the change in
slope, $B_m$, as the size of the boom. The argument for exogeneity is that a sudden break,
unmatched by any break in fundamentals, reflects a shift in buyer expectations rather than a
shift in the local economy. Areas without a real break still get an estimated break, but a tiny
one, and they serve as the control group.

Liao and Mulder use $B_m$ in two ways. An event study compares areas with large and small breaks
in event time around each area's break date, estimated with the local projections
difference-in-differences estimator of @dube2025local because break dates are staggered. Then a
two-stage least squares model instruments log house prices with the break size interacted with
event-time indicators,

$$
\ln \text{HPI}_{mt} = \sum_{k \ge 0} \pi_k\, \mathbb{1}\{t - \tau_m = k\}\, B_m + \mathbf{x}_{mt}'\gamma + \alpha_m + \delta_t + u_{mt},
$$

$$
\text{asinh}(\text{NFIP}_{mt}) = \beta \ln \text{HPI}_{mt} + \mathbf{x}_{mt}'\gamma + \alpha_m + \delta_t + \varepsilon_{mt},
$$

so $\beta$ is a home price elasticity of the number of policies in force. The event-time
interaction lets the instrument trace the whole hump of boom and bust rather than a single jump,
which buys strength and lets the bust half of the cycle be checked against the boom half.

The exclusion restriction is that break size affects insurance demand only through prices. The
paper attacks the obvious violations one at a time. New construction during the boom could raise
policy counts mechanically, so the main outcome is restricted to structures built before 2003.
Mandatory purchase rules in designated floodplains could blur voluntary demand, so the key
specifications use policies outside those zones. Coastal markets had both larger booms and more
flood risk, so the models include property-level flood risk scores interacted with year. And if
rising prices simply meant more expensive structures to insure, building coverage per policy
should rise with the boom; it does not, which works as a placebo outcome. Intensive margins such
as deductible choice and contents coverage are also flat over the cycle, which argues against a
general change in risk preferences.

The simulation below captures the logic and the main way it fails. Local fundamentals move both
prices and insurance demand, so least squares is biased. The break instrument removes that bias,
until boom size is allowed to correlate with an area's flood-risk trend.

```{r vint-break-sim}
library(fixest)
set.seed(2026)

sim_break <- function(n_msa = 300, risk_corr = 0) {
  years <- 2000:2012
  B   <- rexp(n_msa, 3)                          # break size, many near zero
  tau <- sample(2003:2005, n_msa, replace = TRUE)
  risk <- as.numeric(scale(rnorm(n_msa) + risk_corr * scale(B)))
  d <- expand.grid(msa = 1:n_msa, year = years)
  k <- d$year - tau[d$msa]
  hump <- ifelse(k < 0, 0, ifelse(k <= 3, k / 3, pmax(1 - (k - 3) / 4, 0.2)))
  fund <- unsplit(lapply(split(rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 0.03), d$msa), cumsum), d$msa)
  d$lnhpi  <- 0.03 * (d$year - 2000) + 0.8 * B[d$msa] * hump + 0.6 * fund +
              rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 0.01)
  d$lnnfip <- 0.35 * d$lnhpi + 1.0 * fund + 0.02 * risk[d$msa] * (d$year - 2000) +
              rnorm(n_msa)[d$msa] + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 0.02)
  d$kbin <- factor(ifelse(k < 0, "pre", pmin(k, 8)))
  d$B <- B[d$msa]; d$risk <- risk[d$msa]

  ols    <- feols(lnnfip ~ lnhpi | msa + year[risk], d)
  iv_nor <- feols(lnnfip ~ 1 | msa + year | lnhpi ~ i(kbin, B, ref = "pre"), d)
  iv_r   <- feols(lnnfip ~ 1 | msa + year[risk] | lnhpi ~ i(kbin, B, ref = "pre"), d)
  c(ols = coef(ols)[["lnhpi"]],
    iv_no_risk_trend = coef(iv_nor)[["fit_lnhpi"]],
    iv_risk_by_year  = coef(iv_r)[["fit_lnhpi"]],
    first_stage_F    = unname(fitstat(iv_r, "ivwald1")[[1]]$stat))
}

res_break <- t(sapply(c(0, 0.6), function(rc)
  c(boom_risk_correlation = rc, round(rowMeans(replicate(100, sim_break(risk_corr = rc))), 3))))
knitr::kable(res_break, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste("Structural-break instrument, 100 simulated panels of 300 areas.",
                  "True price elasticity of take-up is 0.35."))
```

In the first row, boom size is unrelated to flood risk. Least squares is pulled well above the
truth because local fundamentals raise both prices and insurance demand, while both instrumental
variables estimates sit near 0.35. In the second row, areas with bigger booms also have
faster-rising flood risk. The instrument is as strong as before, with a first-stage $F$ in the
thousands (the simulated boom profile is far cleaner than any real price index), yet without the risk-by-year control the estimate absorbs the risk trend and overshoots.
Including the control restores it, but only because the confound was measured. This is why the
paper's First Street risk scores matter so much: they turn the single most plausible exclusion
violation into an observable that can be partialled out, and the remaining argument is about
confounds that were not measured.

The aggregate design also reveals a hint that the second design is built to test. When the
authors split the bust period by construction year, the price elasticity is several times larger
for homes built in 2003 to 2005 than for older homes. Those owners bought near the peak, so they
had the least equity at the trough. An elasticity that depends on the level of equity, and not
only its change, is what risk shifting predicts and what a pure wealth effect does not.

#### Design Two: Same Shock, Different Stakes

The micro design follows flood insurance policies in force in 2006 and asks which ones were
renewed each year from 2007 to 2012. The obstacle is that the flood insurance records say
nothing about mortgages: no purchase date, no price, no loan. The authors solve this with a
sample restriction that makes the purchase date knowable. They keep only policies on homes that
were built and first insured in the same year, between 2000 and 2005. A house built in 2003 and
first insured in 2003 was almost certainly bought in 2003. That pins down the cohort.

They then merge, by zip code and construction year, the average purchase price and loan-to-value
ratio of new homes from deeds and mortgage records. Purchase price is rolled forward with the
metropolitan price index, the loan balance is amortized on a standard thirty-year schedule, and
the difference is equity in every year. EaR is computed from equity, the insured structure
value, and an empirical distribution of flood losses built from historical claims by state. The
estimating equation is

$$
\text{Renew}_{icmzt} = \beta_1\, \text{Equity}_{icmt} + \beta_2\, \text{EaR}_{icmt} + \alpha_{cmt} + \lambda_{zt} + \varepsilon_{it},
$$

where $c$ is the purchase cohort, $m$ the metropolitan area, and $z$ the zip code.

The fixed effects are the design, so it is worth being precise about what each one removes.
Cohort by area by year effects $\alpha_{cmt}$ absorb everything common to people who bought in
the same market in the same year, including that cohort's exposure to the local price path,
its general renewal trend, and any cohort-level selection into buying at the peak.
Zip-by-year effects $\lambda_{zt}$ absorb everything local in time: neighborhood price changes,
job losses, foreclosure waves, changes in lender behavior, and flood events. What remains is
variation across zip codes within a cohort and market, in the gap between one cohort's equity
path and another's. That is a triple difference: cohort by zip by year. Equity enters linearly
to absorb the wealth channel. Because EaR is a kinked, nonlinear function of equity, it is not
collinear with equity, and $\beta_2$ is identified from where on the kink each cell sits.

The authors show the mechanism the design relies on directly, by regressing EaR on equity
separately for each purchase cohort over 2007 to 2012. For early buyers the slope is close to
zero: they had so much equity that the bust left their flood exposure intact. For 2005 buyers
the slope is several times steeper. This plot is the analogue of a first stage. It shows that
purchase timing changes how a common shock translates into the treatment of interest, and a
reader can see it before any outcome data enter.

Two features of the construction deserve attention. First, equity is assigned from zip-by-cohort
averages, so individual households are measured with error. Because the assignment uses group
means of predetermined terms rather than each household's realized loan, the error is closer to
the grouped, Berkson type than to classical noise, and the authors interpret their coefficients
as intent-to-treat effects of constructed exposure. That is the same logic as a simulated
instrument (Section \@ref(sec-simulated-iv)): a formula applied to predetermined terms and a
common path, purged of later individual choices such as cash-out refinancing. Second, the sample
conditions on holding a policy in 2006, so it describes renewal among the already insured, not
take-up by everyone.

Substantively, the paper finds that lower EaR reduces renewal by much more than the same dollar
change in total equity, and that the effect is concentrated among peak-of-boom buyers. The equity
coefficient is positive but small, consistent with a modest wealth effect. Adding the original
loan-to-value ratio and structure value as controls, and an indicator for negative equity to
separate risk shifting from strategic default, leaves the EaR effect in place.

#### What the Fixed Effects Buy, and What They Do Not

A simulation makes the design concrete. Forty metropolitan areas with booms of different sizes
each contain eight zip codes. Six cohorts buy between 2000 and 2005 at local prices, with
loan-to-value ratios that vary across zip-cohort cells. Renewal from 2007 to 2012 depends on
equity, on EaR, on zip affluence, and on a local bust shock that hits harder where the boom was
bigger. The true effects are 0.01 percentage points per \$1,000 of equity and 0.10 per \$1,000
of EaR.

```{r vint-micro-sim}
sim_vintage <- function(n_msa = 40, n_zip = 8, level_conf = 0, trend_conf = 0,
                        beta_eq = 0.01, beta_ear = 0.10) {
  cohorts <- 2000:2005; years <- 2007:2012
  boom <- runif(n_msa, 0.02, 0.14)               # annual appreciation 2000 to 2006
  hpi <- function(m, t) ifelse(t <= 2006, (1 + boom[m])^(t - 2000),
                               (1 + boom[m])^6 * (1 - 0.75 * boom[m])^(t - 2006))
  cells <- expand.grid(msa = 1:n_msa, zip = 1:n_zip, cohort = cohorts)
  cells$zip_id <- interaction(cells$msa, cells$zip)
  zip_price <- exp(rnorm(n_msa * n_zip, log(180), 0.25))[as.integer(cells$zip_id)]
  cells$p0 <- zip_price * hpi(cells$msa, cells$cohort)
  # v: buyer composition of a zip-cohort cell. Better-off buyers put more down.
  cells$v <- rnorm(nrow(cells))
  cells$ltv0 <- pmin(pmax(0.82 - 0.06 * cells$v + rnorm(nrow(cells), 0, 0.02), 0.5), 0.98)
  cells$structure <- 0.45 * zip_price * runif(nrow(cells), 0.9, 1.1)

  d <- merge(cells, data.frame(year = years))
  value   <- d$p0 * hpi(d$msa, d$year) / hpi(d$msa, d$cohort)
  balance <- d$ltv0 * d$p0 * (1 - 0.015 * (d$year - d$cohort))
  d$equity <- value - balance
  d$ear    <- ear(d$equity, d$structure)
  bust <- (d$year - 2006) / 6
  aff  <- rnorm(n_msa * n_zip)[as.integer(d$zip_id)]
  d$renew <- 80 + 2 * aff + 0.002 * aff * d$p0 - 40 * boom[d$msa] * bust +
    beta_eq * d$equity + beta_ear * d$ear +
    level_conf * 3 * d$v +            # composition shifts renewal levels
    trend_conf * 6 * d$v * bust +     # composition shifts renewal over the bust
    rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 2)
  d
}

est_vintage <- function(d) {
  pooled   <- feols(renew ~ equity + ear | year, d)
  baseline <- feols(renew ~ equity + ear | cohort^msa^year + zip_id^year, d)
  cell_fe  <- feols(renew ~ equity + ear | cohort^msa^year + zip_id^year + zip_id^cohort, d)
  ltv_ctl  <- feols(renew ~ equity + ear + i(year, ltv0, ref = 2007) |
                      cohort^msa^year + zip_id^year + zip_id^cohort, d)
  early <- d[d$cohort <= 2001, ]
  early$ltv_x_bust <- early$ltv0 * (early$year - 2006)
  placebo  <- feols(renew ~ ltv_x_bust | cohort^msa^year + zip_id^year + zip_id^cohort,
                    early)
  c(pooled = coef(pooled)[["ear"]], baseline = coef(baseline)[["ear"]],
    plus_cell_fe = coef(cell_fe)[["ear"]], plus_ltv_by_year = coef(ltv_ctl)[["ear"]],
    early_cohort_placebo = coef(placebo)[[1]])
}

set.seed(11)
d1 <- sim_vintage()
w <- reshape(d1[d1$year %in% c(2007, 2012), c("zip_id", "cohort", "year", "ear", "equity")],
             idvar = c("zip_id", "cohort"), timevar = "year", direction = "wide")
by_cohort <- aggregate(cbind(change_equity = equity.2012 - equity.2007,
                             change_EaR = ear.2012 - ear.2007) ~ cohort, w, mean)
by_cohort$EaR_on_equity_slope <- sapply(split(d1, d1$cohort), function(x)
  coef(feols(ear ~ equity | msa^year, x))[["equity"]])
knitr::kable(by_cohort, digits = 2,
  caption = "Same bust, different stakes: average 2007 to 2012 changes by purchase cohort (thousands of dollars).")
```

The cohort table is the simulated counterpart of the paper's diagnostic. Every cohort loses
roughly the same equity in the bust, and the early cohorts lose almost no EaR. The 2005 cohort
loses a large share of it. The slope of EaR on equity rises with purchase year. That gradient is
the identifying variation.

```{r vint-micro-mc}
scenarios <- list(clean = c(0, 0), composition_in_levels = c(1, 0),
                  composition_in_trends = c(0, 1))
res_vint <- t(sapply(scenarios, function(s)
  round(rowMeans(replicate(40, est_vintage(sim_vintage(level_conf = s[1], trend_conf = s[2])))), 3)))
knitr::kable(res_vint,
  caption = paste("Estimated EaR effect (true value 0.10) across 40 simulated samples per row.",
                  "The last column is the coefficient on initial loan-to-value times years",
                  "into the bust among 2000 and 2001 buyers, which should be zero."))
```

Read the table one row at a time.

In the clean world, pooled least squares with only year effects is biased because zip affluence
and the local bust shock are correlated with both equity and EaR. The paper's baseline
specification removes both and recovers 0.10. So does every richer specification, and the early
cohort placebo is close to zero.

In the second row, the kind of buyer who ends up in a given zip-cohort cell differs in ways that
shift renewal permanently. Better-off buyers made larger down payments, so they have more EaR
and also renew more for unrelated reasons. Neither cohort-by-area-by-year nor zip-by-year
effects remove a zip-by-cohort level difference, and the baseline is biased. Adding zip-by-cohort
effects fixes it, because identification then comes only from how each cell's EaR changes over
the bust, and level differences in who bought where drop out.

The third row is the threat that matters. Here the buyers who took high loan-to-value loans also
become progressively less likely to renew as the bust deepens, for a reason unrelated to EaR:
they are liquidity constrained, or their price expectations soured faster, or they were more
likely to be laid off. This is a composition difference in trends. Zip-by-cohort effects cannot
remove it, and here the estimate is badly wrong, because high loan-to-value cells are exactly the
cells whose EaR fell most. Two tools help. The placebo looks only at the 2000 and 2001 buyers,
whose EaR barely moved: if initial leverage still predicts falling renewal among people for
whom leverage did not change flood exposure, leverage is acting through some other channel, and
the placebo coefficient is far from zero. And controlling for initial loan-to-value interacted
with year forces identification to come only from the curvature of EaR (the part that depends on
structure values and the shape of the loss distribution, not on leverage itself), which recovers
the truth in this simulation. In real data that control spends a great deal of variation, and the
remaining identification rests on the loss distribution being correctly specified. The paper's
robustness column adds loan-to-value and structure value as controls; the simulation suggests
that interacting them with time is the version a referee would ask for.

#### The Recipe

Stripped of the flood setting, the paper's micro design has five ingredients, and each can be
looked for elsewhere.

1.  A predetermined entry date with recorded terms: a purchase, origination, grant, hire,
    enrollment, or contract signing, along with the price, rate, or leverage fixed at that date.
2.  A common path after entry that individual units cannot influence: a local price index, a
    market interest rate, a share price, an exchange rate, or a business cycle.
3.  A known mapping from entry terms and path to the state of interest, preferably with a kink,
    a cap, or an option-like nonlinearity, so that the same path produces different changes in
    the state for different vintages.
4.  Fixed effects for the path (location by time) and for the vintage (cohort by location by
    time), so that neither the shock nor selection into a vintage identifies the effect; only
    their interaction does.
5.  A competing channel that moves with the path in a simpler way, entered as a control (here,
    total equity), so the nonlinear component can be read as a separate mechanism.

The same structure appears in published work across household finance and labor economics.

| Setting | Entry terms | Common path | Constructed state | Reference |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Flood insurance renewal | Purchase year, loan-to-value | Metropolitan price index | Equity-at-risk | @liao2026whats |
| Labor supply | Purchase timing within zip code | Local price index | Negative equity | @bernstein2021negative |
| Home improvement | Loan terms at purchase | Local price index | Debt overhang | @melzer2017mortgage |
| Residential mobility | Origination rate | Market mortgage rate | Rate gap (lock-in) | @fonseca2024mortgage; @liebersohn2025household |
| Early careers | Graduation year | Business cycle | Entry conditions | @oreopoulos2012short; @schwandt2019unlucky |

The recipe also suggests designs that, as far as this book knows, are open. Subscription
businesses that grandfather old prices create customer cohorts whose effective discount relative
to the list price is fixed by sign-up date and moved by later price changes, which is a vintage
design for price sensitivity of churn. Employee stock options granted on different dates are
pushed in or out of the money by the same share price path, which separates the incentive effect
of moneyness from the wealth effect of the share price. Firms that issued fixed-rate debt at
different dates face the same rate path with different refinancing gains. In each case the
first question is whether a mapping like EaR exists, with a region where the path does nothing to
the state, because that region supplies the placebo.

#### How It Relates to the Other Families

Design one is a shift-share argument in disguise. The share is an area's break size and the shift
is a common event-time profile, and the identification rests on the breaks being as good as
randomly assigned with respect to unmeasured trends in insurance demand
(Section \@ref(sec-shift-share-iv)). Design two is closer to a simulated instrument
(Section \@ref(sec-simulated-iv)), because EaR is a formula evaluated on predetermined terms and
a common path, deliberately ignoring what each household later did. Its reliance on curvature
connects it to the regression kink design (Section \@ref(sec-regression-kink-design)), with the
difference that the kink here sits at a different place for every cell. And the use of an
aggregate shock that lands differently by timing is a cousin of the timing instrument in
Section \@ref(sec-examiner-timing-iv).

#### Practice

1.  Name the path and the vintage separately, and show that the fixed effects absorb each one
    alone. If the effect is still identified when either is dropped from the interaction, the
    design is leaning on something else.
2.  Plot the mapping by cohort before showing any outcomes. The cohort-specific slope of the
    constructed state on the common shock is the first stage of this design, and it should be
    flat for vintages where the mechanism cannot bind.
3.  Use those flat vintages as a placebo. Entry terms that predict outcome trends where the
    constructed state did not move are evidence of a competing channel.
4.  Add zip-by-cohort (or unit) effects so that composition in levels drops out, and interact
    initial terms with time so that composition in trends drops out too. Report how much
    identifying variation is left after each step.
5.  Report sensitivity to the parts of the mapping that are assumed rather than observed: the
    amortization schedule, the loss distribution, the structure value. Identification from
    curvature is only as good as the curve.
6.  Cluster at the level at which the common path varies, here the metropolitan area, and say how
    many clusters that leaves.
7.  State the conditioning. A sample of renewing policyholders, or of firms that survived to the
    shock, answers a narrower question than the population one.

#### Applications

The finding reshapes who bears flood risk. Highly leveraged owners in flood-exposed homes who
stop insuring transfer part of their expected losses to lenders, and through securitization to
the government-sponsored enterprises that buy those mortgages and, outside designated floodplains,
neither price flood risk nor require coverage. For a mortgage investor or a regulator stress
testing climate exposure, the implication is that uninsured flood losses are concentrated
precisely in the high loan-to-value loans written near price peaks, and that a price decline
raises that exposure twice: once through lower collateral values and again through lapsed
insurance. For an insurer or the flood insurance program, renewal models that ignore borrower
equity will over-predict retention after a housing downturn among the newest buyers.

The method carries over to disputes and consulting work wherever a common shock hits a book of
contracts signed at different dates. An expert asked whether a price change, a rate change, or a
policy change caused customers to leave can often reconstruct each contract's exposure from its
signing terms and the common path, then use vintage-by-time and location-by-time fixed effects to
show the response follows the constructed exposure and not merely the shock. The placebo on
vintages that the shock could not have affected is usually the most persuasive single exhibit,
because it answers the opposing expert's natural reply that the affected customers were simply
different.
